title: Εὐχὴ Ἀχιλλέως
titleEn: The Prayer of Achilles and the Fire Quenched — Iliad 16.210–305
part: The Prayer of Achilles and the Fire Quenched (16.210–305)
about: Achilles ends his speech and the Myrmidon ranks close up like a wall. Patroclus and Automedon arm in front of them, and Achilles goes to his hut, opens the chest his mother packed, and takes out the cup from which no one else drinks and from which wine is poured to no god but Zeus. He cleanses it, washes his hands, and pours wine standing in the enclosure, praying that Zeus give Patroclus glory and bring him back safe with his armour and companions. Zeus grants the first half of the prayer and refuses the second. The Myrmidons pour out from the ships like wasps stirred up by boys, and Patroclus calls on them to honour Achilles so that Agamemnon may know his folly. The Trojans waver at the sight of the two in gleaming gear, Patroclus makes the first cast and kills the Paeonian leader Pyraechmes, drives the Trojans from the ships and puts out the fire. The Danaans surge out, and the poet likens the lull to a cloud lifted from a mountain, though the Trojans have not yet been routed.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὄτρυνε μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἑκάστου.
sentences.l: So having spoken, he urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes Achilles’ speech, which ended at line 209, and the whole line is a stock one for a leader who has finished rousing his men; it stands also at 5.470 and 13.155. ὄτρυνε is ὤτρυνε without the augment, from ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, and has two objects, μένος ‘might’ and θυμόν ‘heart’, the pair that make a man’s fighting spirit; ἑκάστου ‘of each’ depends on both. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: μᾶλλον δὲ στίχες ἄρθεν, ἐπεὶ βασιλῆος ἄκουσαν.
sentences.l: And more closely the ranks were fitted together, when they heard the king.
sentences.i: And the ranks closed up all the more tightly when they heard their king.
sentences.n: μᾶλλον ‘all the more’ goes with the verb. ἄρθεν has no augment and is read as the aorist passive of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit together’, the verb of the simile that follows, so that the ranks ‘were fitted together’; it could instead be from ἀείρω ‘lift’, and the simile favours the first. στίχες are ‘ranks’. ἐπεὶ βασιλῆος ἄκουσαν is ‘when they heard the king’: βασιλῆος is the epic genitive after ἀκούω, and ἄκουσαν lacks the augment. The king is Achilles.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε τοῖχον ἀνὴρ ἀράρῃ πυκινοῖσι λίθοισι
δώματος ὑψηλοῖο βίας ἀνέμων ἀλεείνων,
ὣς ἄραρον κόρυθές τε καὶ ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι.
sentences.l:
And as when a man fits together a wall with solid stones
of a high house, shunning the force of the winds,
so were fitted together the helmets and the bossed shields.
sentences.i: As when a man fits together the wall of a high house with close-set stones, shunning the force of the winds, so the helmets and the bossed shields were fitted together.
sentences.n: The simile of the wall. ὡς δ’ ὅτε ‘and as when’ takes the subjunctive ἀράρῃ, from ἀραρίσκω ‘fit together’; τοῖχον is the wall, and πυκινοῖσι λίθοισι ‘with solid stones’ is epic -οισι for Attic -οις. δώματος ὑψηλοῖο ‘of a high house’ says whose wall, and ἀλεείνων ‘shunning’ has βίας ἀνέμων ‘the force of the winds’ as its object. ὣς ἄραρον ‘so were fitted’ answers: ἄραρον is a past form of the same verb, without the augment, standing with no object: the helmets and shields fitted together.

sentences.t: ἀσπὶς ἄρ’ ἀσπίδ’ ἔρειδε, κόρυς κόρυν, ἀνέρα δ’ ἀνήρ·
sentences.l: shield pressed on shield, helmet on helmet, and man on man;
sentences.i: shield pressed on shield, helmet on helmet, man on man;
sentences.n: The packing of the line. ἀσπίς, κόρυς and ἀνήρ are each the subject of ἔρειδε, the imperfect of ἐρείδω ‘press, lean’, with its own accusative (ἀσπίδ’ and κόρυν after their verb, ἀνέρα before its subject), so each thing leans on its like. ἀσπίς ‘shield’ and κόρυς ‘helmet’ are the ordinary words. Lines 215–217 repeat 13.131–133.

sentences.t:
ψαῦον δ’ ἱππόκομοι κόρυθες λαμπροῖσι φάλοισι
νευόντων, ὡς πυκνοὶ ἐφέστασαν ἀλλήλοισι.
sentences.l:
and the horse-plumed helmets touched with their bright ridges
as the men nodded, so close they were standing to one another.
sentences.i: and the helmets with horsehair plumes touched one another with their bright ridges as the men nodded, so closely did they stand to one another.
sentences.n: Helmet touching helmet. ψαῦον is the imperfect of ψαύω ‘touch’, with no object stated, since the helmets touch one another. ἱππόκομοι κόρυθες is ‘horse-plumed helmets’, and φάλοισι is the dative of φάλος, taken to be the ridge of the helmet that carries the plume (the sense is not certain). νευόντων is the genitive plural of the participle of νεύω ‘nod’, with an unspoken ‘of the men’. ὡς πυκνοὶ ἐφέστασαν ἀλλήλοισι is ‘how closely they stood against one another’, ἐφέστασαν an epic past of ἐφίστημι.

sentences.t:
πάντων δὲ προπάροιθε δύ’ ἀνέρε θωρήσσοντο
Πάτροκλός τε καὶ Αὐτομέδων ἕνα θυμὸν ἔχοντες
πρόσθεν Μυρμιδόνων πολεμιζέμεν.
sentences.l:
And before them all two men were arming themselves,
Patroclus and Automedon, having one heart,
in front of the Myrmidons to fight.
sentences.i: And in front of them all two men were arming themselves, Patroclus and Automedon, with one heart between them, to fight in front of the Myrmidons.
sentences.n: Two men are named as the front pair. θωρήσσοντο is the imperfect middle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’, so ‘were arming themselves’, and δύ’ ἀνέρε is a dual, ‘two men’. ἕνα θυμὸν ἔχοντες ‘having one heart’ means being of one mind. πρόσθεν Μυρμιδόνων ‘in front of the Myrmidons’ goes with πολεμιζέμεν, the epic infinitive of πολεμίζω ‘fight’ (Attic πολεμίζειν), which says what they armed for. The unit ends mid-line, at the full stop in line 220.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν ἐς κλισίην, χηλοῦ δ’ ἀπὸ πῶμ’ ἀνέῳγε
καλῆς δαιδαλέης,
sentences.l:
But Achilles
set out to go to his hut, and from the chest the lid he opened,
fair, wrought,
sentences.i: But Achilles set out for his hut, and opened the lid of the fair, finely wrought chest,
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ turns from the ranks to Achilles. βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν is ‘set out to go’, βῆ with an infinitive, and ῥ’ is ἄρα. ἀνέῳγε is a past form of ἀνοίγνυμι ‘open’ (formally a pluperfect, used as a simple past), with πῶμα ‘lid’ as its object; ἀπό stands after its noun, χηλοῦ δ’ ἀπό, ‘from the chest’. καλῆς δαιδαλέης ‘fair, wrought’ is a genitive agreeing with χηλοῦ, held over to the next line. The unit is cut at a comma, because the sentence runs on to line 224.

sentences.t:
τήν οἱ Θέτις ἀργυρόπεζα
θῆκ’ ἐπὶ νηὸς ἄγεσθαι ἐῢ πλήσασα χιτώνων
χλαινάων τ’ ἀνεμοσκεπέων οὔλων τε ταπήτων.
sentences.l:
which for him Thetis, silver-footed,
put on the ship, to be taken along, having filled it well with tunics
and wind-sheltering cloaks and thick rugs.
sentences.i: which silver-footed Thetis had put on his ship for him to take with him, filling it well with tunics, cloaks to shelter from the wind, and thick rugs.
sentences.n: τήν ‘which’ is the relative and looks back to the chest; οἱ is ‘for him’. θῆκ’ is θῆκε, the aorist of τίθημι; ἐπὶ νηός ‘on the ship’ is a genitive, and ἄγεσθαι the middle infinitive ‘to take along (for himself)’. ἐῢ πλήσασα ‘filling it well’ takes the genitive of what fills it: χιτώνων ‘tunics’, χλαινάων … ἀνεμοσκεπέων ‘wind-sheltering cloaks’ (-άων is the epic genitive plural; ἀνεμοσκεπής is built on ἄνεμος ‘wind’ and the root of σκέπας ‘shelter’), and οὔλων … ταπήτων ‘thick rugs’. ἀργυρόπεζα is the stock ‘silver-footed’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δέ οἱ δέπας ἔσκε τετυγμένον, οὐδέ τις ἄλλος
οὔτ’ ἀνδρῶν πίνεσκεν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ αἴθοπα οἶνον,
οὔτέ τεῳ σπένδεσκε θεῶν, ὅτε μὴ Διὶ πατρί.
sentences.l:
And there for him was a cup, well-wrought, and no other
of men used to drink from it the fire-faced wine,
nor to any of the gods used to pour libation, except to father Zeus.
sentences.i: And there he had a well-wrought cup, and no one else of men used to drink the wine that has the look of fire from it, or used to pour libation to any of the gods, except to father Zeus.
sentences.n: ἔσκε is a Homeric form of ἦν ‘was’, and τετυγμένον is the perfect passive participle of τεύχω ‘make’, so ‘a well-wrought cup’. οὐδέ τις ἄλλος and the pair οὔτ’ … οὔτε make a long negative: no other man drank, and nobody poured libation to a god, but for Zeus. πίνεσκεν and σπένδεσκε are forms in -σκ-, ‘used to drink’, ‘used to pour libation’. τεῳ is Ionic τινι ‘to anyone’, and ὅτε μή here means ‘except’. αἴθοπα οἶνον ‘fire-faced wine’ is a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
τό ῥα τότ’ ἐκ χηλοῖο λαβὼν ἐκάθηρε θεείῳ
πρῶτον, ἔπειτα δ’ ἔνιψ’ ὕδατος καλῇσι ῥοῇσι,
νίψατο δ’ αὐτὸς χεῖρας, ἀφύσσατο δ’ αἴθοπα οἶνον.
sentences.l:
This then, from the chest taking it, he cleansed with sulphur
first, and then washed with the fair streams of water,
and washed his hands himself, and drew up the fire-faced wine.
sentences.i: Taking it from the chest, he cleansed it first with sulphur, and then washed it in the fair streams of water, and washed his own hands, and drew up the wine that has the look of fire.
sentences.n: τό ῥα τότ’ is τὸ ἄρα τότε, ‘this then’, the cup; ἐκ χηλοῖο λαβών is ‘taking it out of the chest’, with the epic genitive -οιο. ἐκάθηρε is the aorist of καθαίρω ‘cleanse’, and θεείῳ is the dative of θέειον ‘sulphur’. πρῶτον … ἔπειτα ‘first … then’ orders the steps. ἔνιψ’ is ἔνιψε, aorist of νίζω ‘wash’, and νίψατο the aorist middle, ‘washed for himself’, with χεῖρας as its object. ἀφύσσατο is the aorist middle of ἀφύσσω ‘draw up’, here the wine, for himself.

sentences.t:
εὔχετ’ ἔπειτα στὰς μέσῳ ἕρκεϊ, λεῖβε δὲ οἶνον
οὐρανὸν εἰσανιδών·
sentences.l:
He prayed then, standing in the middle of the enclosure, and poured the wine
looking up at heaven;
sentences.i: Then he stood in the middle of the enclosure and prayed, and poured the wine as he looked up at heaven;
sentences.n: εὔχετ’ is the imperfect of εὔχομαι, which of a request to a god means ‘pray’. στάς is the aorist participle of ἵστημι, ‘having taken his stand’, and μέσῳ ἕρκεϊ is ‘in the middle of the enclosure’, the fenced space (ἕρκος); the Greek does not say whose. λεῖβε is the imperfect of λείβω ‘pour’, here the libation of wine, and οἶνον is its object. εἰσανιδών is an aorist participle, ‘looking up at’, built on εἰς, ἀνά and the root of ἰδεῖν ‘see’, and οὐρανόν ‘heaven’ is its object. The ano teleia ends the unit mid-line.

sentences.t: Δία δ’ οὐ λάθε τερπικέραυνον·
sentences.l: and Zeus, delighting-in-the-thunderbolt, he did not escape;
sentences.i: and he did not escape the notice of Zeus, who delights in the thunderbolt;
sentences.n: Δία is the accusative of Ζεύς and the object of λάθε, the aorist of λανθάνω without the augment: ‘he did not escape Zeus’, that is, the god noticed. The subject is not stated; it is Achilles. τερπικέραυνον ‘who delights in the thunderbolt’ is a stock epithet of Zeus, translated every time. The prayer follows in the next line.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ ἄνα Δωδωναῖε Πελασγικὲ τηλόθι ναίων
Δωδώνης μεδέων δυσχειμέρου, ἀμφὶ δὲ Σελλοὶ
σοὶ ναίουσ’ ὑποφῆται ἀνιπτόποδες χαμαιεῦναι,
sentences.l:
“Zeus, lord, of Dodona, Pelasgian, dwelling far away,
ruling over Dodona, harsh-wintered, and around, the Selli
dwell, your interpreters, with unwashed feet, sleeping on the ground,
sentences.i: “Lord Zeus of Dodona, Pelasgian, you who dwell far away, you who rule over Dodona of the harsh winters, around you dwell the Selli, your interpreters, with unwashed feet, who sleep on the ground,
sentences.n: The prayer begins here and runs to the end of line 248. Ζεῦ ἄνα is ‘lord Zeus’, and Δωδωναῖε ‘of Dodona’ and Πελασγικέ ‘Pelasgian’ are vocative adjectives; the Pelasgians are a people named elsewhere in the poem, and why the god bears the name is not said. μεδέων is the participle of μεδέω ‘rule over’, with the genitive Δωδώνης; δυσχείμερος is ‘of the harsh winters’. ἀμφί is an adverb, ‘around’, Σελλοί ‘the Selli’ the subject of ναίουσ’ (ναίουσι), and ὑποφῆται ‘interpreters’ those who speak for the god; σοί ‘for you’ says whose interpreters they are, and the English has ‘your’ (and ‘around you’ with ἀμφί). ἀνιπτόποδες ‘with unwashed feet’ and χαμαιεῦναι ‘sleeping on the ground’ (χαμαί + εὐνή) describe them.

sentences.t:
ἠμὲν δή ποτ’ ἐμὸν ἔπος ἔκλυες εὐξαμένοιο,
τίμησας μὲν ἐμέ, μέγα δ’ ἴψαο λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν,
sentences.l:
both once indeed my word you heard, when I prayed,
you honoured me, and greatly struck the people of the Achaeans,
sentences.i: as once you heard my word when I prayed, and honoured me, and struck the people of the Achaeans hard,
sentences.n: ἠμέν … ἠδ’ ‘both … and’ is the pair that joins this to the next unit: both what the god once did and what is now asked. δή ποτε is ‘once indeed’. ἔκλυες is the aorist of κλύω ‘hear’, with ἐμὸν ἔπος ‘my word’ as object and εὐξαμένοιο, a genitive agreeing with an unspoken ‘me’, ‘when I prayed’. τίμησας μὲν ἐμέ is ‘you honoured me’. ἴψαο is the aorist middle of ἴπτω, a rare verb; ‘strike hard’ is its traditional sense, and the Greek does not say how the Achaeans were struck. The unit is cut at the comma.

sentences.t: ἠδ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν μοι τόδ’ ἐπικρήηνον ἐέλδωρ·
sentences.l: and still, even now, for me this fulfil, the wish;
sentences.i: and further, even now, fulfil this wish for me;
sentences.n: ἠδ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν is ‘and still, even now’, the second half of the ἠμέν … ἠδ’ pair begun in the line before. ἐπικρήηνον is the aorist imperative of ἐπικραιαίνω ‘bring to pass, fulfil’, and ἐέλδωρ ‘wish’ is its object, with τόδε ‘this’ and μοι ‘for me’; the wish itself comes in the lines that follow. The same line stands at 1.455.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς μὲν γὰρ ἐγὼ μενέω νηῶν ἐν ἀγῶνι,
ἀλλ’ ἕταρον πέμπω πολέσιν μετὰ Μυρμιδόνεσσι
μάρνασθαι·
sentences.i: For I myself shall stay in the gathering-place of the ships, but I am sending my companion among the many Myrmidons to fight;
sentences.n: αὐτὸς μὲν … ἀλλά sets Achilles’ own staying against his sending. μενέω is the future of μένω ‘stay’, and νηῶν ἐν ἀγῶνι is ‘in the gathering-place of the ships’, ἀγών being a place where men gather. ἕταρον ‘companion’ is Patroclus, left unnamed and without a ‘my’ in the Greek; πολέσιν μετὰ Μυρμιδόνεσσι is ‘among the many Myrmidons’ (πολέσιν the epic dative plural of πολύς), and μάρνασθαι ‘to fight’ is an infinitive of purpose after πέμπω. The ano teleia ends the unit mid-line.

sentences.t:
τῷ κῦδος ἅμα πρόες εὐρύοπα Ζεῦ,
θάρσυνον δέ οἱ ἦτορ ἐνὶ φρεσίν,
sentences.l:
therefore glory along with him send, far-thundering Zeus,
and cheer for him the heart within his wits,
sentences.i: so send glory with him, Zeus who thunders from afar, and cheer the heart in his mind,
sentences.n: τῷ is read as ‘therefore’; it could be the dative ‘to him’, but the οἱ of the next clause is more natural beside ‘therefore’. κῦδος ‘glory’ is the object of πρόες, the aorist imperative of προΐημι ‘send forth’, and ἅμα ‘along’ goes with it. εὐρύοπα is a stock epithet of Zeus: ‘far-thundering’ is the traditional explanation, and the second half of the word is disputed. θάρσυνον is the imperative of θαρσύνω ‘cheer’, with οἱ ‘for him’ and ἦτορ ‘heart’; ἐνὶ φρεσίν is ‘in his wits’, the mind. The unit ends mid-line, at the comma after φρεσίν.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα καὶ Ἕκτωρ
εἴσεται ἤ ῥα καὶ οἶος ἐπίστηται πολεμίζειν
ἡμέτερος θεράπων, ἦ οἱ τότε χεῖρες ἄαπτοι
μαίνονθ’, ὁππότ’ ἐγώ περ ἴω μετὰ μῶλον Ἄρηος.
sentences.l:
so that Hector too
will know whether even alone he knows how to fight,
this attendant of ours, or whether his hands, then, invincible,
rage, whenever I myself go among the toil of Ares.
sentences.i: so that Hector too will find out whether our attendant knows how to fight even alone, or whether his invincible hands rage then, whenever I myself go into the toil of battle.
sentences.n: ὄφρα with the future εἴσεται (of οἶδα ‘know’) gives purpose: ‘so that he will know’. ἤ … ἦ … is ‘whether … or whether’. ἐπίστηται is the subjunctive of ἐπίσταμαι ‘know how to’, and οἶος is ‘alone’; ἡμέτερος θεράπων is ‘our attendant’, Patroclus. The second alternative is that his χεῖρες ἄαπτοι ‘invincible hands’ μαίνονθ’ (μαίνονται) ‘rage’ only with Achilles in the fight: περ stresses ἐγώ, and ἴω is the subjunctive of εἶμι ‘go’. μῶλον Ἄρηος ‘the toil of Ares’ is battle.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί κ’ ἀπὸ ναῦφι μάχην ἐνοπήν τε δίηται,
ἀσκηθής μοι ἔπειτα θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας ἵκοιτο
τεύχεσί τε ξὺν πᾶσι καὶ ἀγχεμάχοις ἑτάροισιν.
sentences.l:
But when from the ships he has driven battle and the shouting,
unscathed, for me, then to the swift ships may he come
with his armour, all of it, and his close-fighting companions.”
sentences.i: But when he has driven battle and its shouting away from the ships, may he come back to me unscathed to the swift ships, with all his armour and his close-fighting companions.”
sentences.n: ἐπεί κε with the subjunctive is ‘when … he shall have’; δίηται is the subjunctive middle of δίημι ‘drive away’, and its objects are μάχην ἐνοπήν τε ‘battle and the shouting’. ἀπὸ ναῦφι is ‘from the ships’, -φι being an old ending. ἵκοιτο is the optative of wish, ‘may he come’, with ἀσκηθής ‘unscathed’ and μοι ‘for me’; τεύχεσί τε ξὺν πᾶσι is ‘with all his armour’ (ξύν is σύν), and ἀγχεμάχοις ἑτάροισιν ‘close-fighting companions’ are the Myrmidons. The prayer ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος, τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε μητίετα Ζεύς.
sentences.l: So he spoke, praying, and him heard counsellor Zeus.
sentences.i: So he prayed, and Zeus the counsellor heard him.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος ‘so he spoke, praying’ closes a prayer, and τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε ‘and heard him’ takes the genitive of the one heard; κλύω says no more than ‘hear’, and the next lines tell how much was granted. μητίετα ‘counsellor’ is a stock epithet of Zeus, translated every time. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἕτερον μὲν ἔδωκε πατήρ, ἕτερον δ’ ἀνένευσε·
sentences.l: To him the one thing the father gave, the other he refused with a sign;
sentences.i: The father gave him the one thing, but the other he refused with a sign;
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘to him’. ἕτερον μὲν … ἕτερον δέ is ‘the one thing … the other’, the two halves of the prayer set against each other: the first is given, the second refused. ἀνένευσε is the aorist of ἀνανεύω, literally ‘throw the head back’, the sign of refusal, and here it takes an object, so ‘refused with a sign’. πατήρ ‘the father’ is Zeus, as the Διὶ πατρί of the lines before was. The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t:
νηῶν μέν οἱ ἀπώσασθαι πόλεμόν τε μάχην τε
δῶκε, σόον δ’ ἀνένευσε μάχης ἐξαπονέεσθαι.
sentences.l:
To thrust war and battle away from the ships
he gave him, but to come back safe from the battle he refused with a sign.
sentences.i: He granted him to thrust war and battle away from the ships, but that he should come back from the fighting safe he refused with a sign.
sentences.n: The two halves are now spelled out. ἀπώσασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of ἀπωθέω ‘thrust away’, depending on δῶκε ‘gave’; νηῶν ‘from the ships’ and the objects πόλεμον and μάχην ‘war’ and ‘battle’ go with it, and οἱ is ‘to him’. In the second half σόον is the accusative of σῶς ‘safe’, agreeing with the unspoken subject of the infinitive ἐξαπονέεσθαι ‘to come back out’ (ἐξ + ἀπό + νέομαι), and μάχης is the genitive ‘from battle’. What is refused is Patroclus’ return.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὃ μὲν σπείσας τε καὶ εὐξάμενος Διὶ πατρὶ
ἂψ κλισίην εἰσῆλθε, δέπας δ’ ἀπέθηκ’ ἐνὶ χηλῷ,
στῆ δὲ πάροιθ’ ἐλθὼν κλισίης, ἔτι δ’ ἤθελε θυμῷ
εἰσιδέειν Τρώων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν φύλοπιν αἰνήν.
sentences.l:
Truly he, on the one hand, having poured libation and prayed to father Zeus,
back into his hut went, and the cup he put away in the chest,
and stood, having come in front of the hut, and still he wished in his heart
to look upon the fearsome battle-din of Trojans and Achaeans.
sentences.i: He, for his part, when he had poured libation and prayed to father Zeus, went back into his hut and put the cup away in the chest, and came out and stood in front of the hut; and still he wished in his heart to look upon the fearsome din of battle between the Trojans and the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἤτοι (printed as one word) ὃ μὲν is ‘he, for his part’. σπείσας and εὐξάμενος are aorist participles, ‘having poured libation and prayed’, with Διὶ πατρί ‘to father Zeus’. ἂψ ‘back’ goes with εἰσῆλθε, ἀπέθηκ’ is ἀπέθηκε ‘put away’, and ἐνὶ χηλῷ ‘in the chest’ is the chest of line 221. στῆ is ἔστη ‘stood’, with πάροιθ’ … κλισίης ‘in front of the hut’, the genitive separated from its preposition by ἐλθών ‘having come’. ἔτι δ’ ἤθελε θυμῷ ‘and still he wished in his heart’ takes εἰσιδέειν, an epic infinitive ‘to look upon’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἅμα Πατρόκλῳ μεγαλήτορι θωρηχθέντες
ἔστιχον, ὄφρ’ ἐν Τρωσὶ μέγα φρονέοντες ὄρουσαν.
sentences.l:
And they, together with great-spirited Patroclus, having armed themselves,
marched, until among the Trojans, thinking great things, they leapt.
sentences.i: And they, armed together with great-spirited Patroclus, marched on until they sprang in among the Trojans, with high thoughts.
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the Myrmidons. θωρηχθέντες is the aorist passive participle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’, ‘having armed themselves’, and ἔστιχον the imperfect of στείχω ‘march’. ὄφρα here is ‘until’, with the aorist ὄρουσαν ‘rushed, sprang’, and ἐν Τρωσί ‘among the Trojans’ is the dative plural Τρωσί. μέγα φρονέοντες ‘thinking great things’ is the participle of φρονέω with μέγα ‘greatly’; the tone, whether pride or confidence, is not decided. μεγαλήτορι ‘great-spirited’ is a stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δὲ σφήκεσσιν ἐοικότες ἐξεχέοντο
εἰνοδίοις, οὓς παῖδες ἐριδμαίνωσιν ἔθοντες
αἰεὶ κερτομέοντες ὁδῷ ἔπι οἰκί’ ἔχοντας
νηπίαχοι·
sentences.l:
And at once, like wasps, they poured out,
wayside ones, which boys provoke, being used to it,
always taunting them, by the road, as they have their dwellings,
childish ones;
sentences.i: And at once they poured out like wayside wasps, which boys, being used to it, provoke, always teasing them beside the road where they have their homes, childish as they are;
sentences.n: ἐξεχέοντο is the imperfect passive of ἐκχέω ‘pour out’, said of the Myrmidons, and σφήκεσσιν ἐοικότες is ‘like wasps’. εἰνοδίοις ‘by the road’, built on ἐν and ὁδός, says where the wasps nest. ἐριδμαίνωσιν is a subjunctive in a relative clause, ‘provoke’ (the verb is built on ἔρις ‘strife’; the exact formation is not certain), and ἔθοντες, from ἔθω ‘be used to’, says it is the boys’ habit. κερτομέοντες ‘taunting’ is said of the boys, and οἰκί’ ἔχοντας ‘having their dwellings’ of the wasps; νηπίαχοι ‘childish’ agrees with the boys.

sentences.t: ξυνὸν δὲ κακὸν πολέεσσι τιθεῖσι.
sentences.l: and a common evil for many they set.
sentences.i: and they set an evil that is common to many.
sentences.n: The boys are the subject. τιθεῖσι is the epic form of τιθέασι ‘they set’, and ξυνόν ‘common’, the shared thing, agrees with κακόν ‘an evil’; πολέεσσι ‘for many’ is the epic dative plural of πολύς. The point is that the harm falls on anyone, as the next lines show. The unit begins in the middle of line 262, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ εἴ περ παρά τίς τε κιὼν ἄνθρωπος ὁδίτης
κινήσῃ ἀέκων, οἳ δ’ ἄλκιμον ἦτορ ἔχοντες
πρόσσω πᾶς πέτεται καὶ ἀμύνει οἷσι τέκεσσι.
sentences.l:
And them, if some man, a wayfarer, going by
should stir them, unwilling, they, a sturdy heart having,
forward each flies and defends its own young.
sentences.i: And if some man, a traveller, passing by, stirs them without meaning to, each of them, keeping a sturdy heart, flies forward and defends its own young.
sentences.n: τούς ‘them’, the wasps, is the object of κινήσῃ, the subjunctive after εἴ περ; ἄνθρωπος ὁδίτης is ‘a man, a traveller’, and παρά … κιών ‘going past’ has κιών from κίω ‘go’. ἀέκων ‘unwilling’ means he does it without meaning to. οἳ δέ ‘they’ takes up the wasps for the main clause, with ἄλκιμον ἦτορ ἔχοντες ‘keeping a sturdy heart’. πᾶς ‘each’ is singular, picking out one wasp at a time; πέτεται is ‘flies’, πρόσσω ‘forward’, and ἀμύνει takes the dative: οἷσι τέκεσσι ‘for its own young’, where οἷσι is the possessive ὅς, not the relative.

sentences.t:
τῶν τότε Μυρμιδόνες κραδίην καὶ θυμὸν ἔχοντες
ἐκ νηῶν ἐχέοντο·
sentences.l:
Of these then the Myrmidons, the heart and spirit having,
from the ships poured out;
sentences.i: With the heart and spirit of those wasps, the Myrmidons then poured out from the ships;
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of those’, the wasps, depends on κραδίην καὶ θυμόν, so that the men have the wasps’ heart and spirit. The simile is now turned back to the Myrmidons in one line. ἐχέοντο is the imperfect passive of χέω ‘pour’, the verb of ἐξεχέοντο at line 259, with ἐκ ‘out of’ here standing with νηῶν. The ano teleia ends the unit mid-line.

sentences.t: βοὴ δ’ ἄσβεστος ὀρώρει.
sentences.l: and an unquenchable war-cry had arisen.
sentences.i: and a war-cry that would never go out had arisen.
sentences.n: βοή is the shout of battle, here a war-cry. ἄσβεστος is ἀ- ‘not’ with the root of σβέννυμι ‘quench’, so literally ‘unquenchable’, and the English puts it as a cry ‘that would never go out’, as for other things that do not die down. ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι (intransitive), ‘had arisen’, a state already there as the men came out.

sentences.t: Πάτροκλος δ’ ἑτάροισιν ἐκέκλετο μακρὸν ἀΰσας·
sentences.l: And Patroclus to his companions called out, shouting loudly:
sentences.i: And Patroclus gave orders to his companions, shouting loudly:
sentences.n: Patroclus now speaks to the men. ἐκέκλετο is the aorist of κέλομαι ‘call, urge’, and the English has ‘gave orders’ for it, as in other speech introductions; what follows is an exhortation as well as an order. μακρὸν ἀΰσας ‘shouting loudly’ is the aorist participle of ἀΰω ‘shout’, with μακρόν ‘long’ used as an adverb. ἑτάροισιν is the dative plural ‘to his companions’.

sentences.t:
Μυρμιδόνες ἕταροι Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος
ἀνέρες ἔστε φίλοι, μνήσασθε δὲ θούριδος ἀλκῆς,
sentences.l:
“Myrmidons, companions of Peleus’-son Achilles,
men be, friends, and be mindful of impetuous might,
sentences.i: “Myrmidons, companions of Achilles, son of Peleus: be men, friends, and remember impetuous might,
sentences.n: The speech begins here and runs to the end of line 274. Μυρμιδόνες is a vocative, with ἕταροι Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος ‘companions of Achilles, son of Peleus’ in apposition (Πηληϊάδεω is the epic genitive of the patronymic Πηληϊάδης). ἀνέρες ἔστε is ‘be men’, ἔστε the imperative of εἰμί, and φίλοι ‘friends’ is a second vocative. μνήσασθε is the aorist imperative middle of μιμνήσκομαι ‘remember’, with the genitive θούριδος ἀλκῆς ‘impetuous might’. Line 270 stands also at 6.112.

sentences.t:
ὡς ἂν Πηλεΐδην τιμήσομεν, ὃς μέγ’ ἄριστος
Ἀργείων παρὰ νηυσὶ καὶ ἀγχέμαχοι θεράποντες,
sentences.l:
so that we may honour Peleus’-son, who is by far the best
of the Argives at the ships, and we, close-fighting attendants,
sentences.i: so that we may honour the son of Peleus, who is by far the best of the Argives at the ships, and we, his close-fighting attendants,
sentences.n: ὡς ἂν … τιμήσομεν is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive in its short-vowel form (Attic τιμήσωμεν), ‘so that we may honour’. Πηλεΐδην is the patronymic again, for Achilles. ὃς μέγ’ ἄριστος has no verb: ‘who is by far the best’, with Ἀργείων παρὰ νηυσί ‘of the Argives at the ships’. ἀγχέμαχοι θεράποντες is nominative, so ‘we, close-fighting attendants’: the Myrmidons name themselves his attendants. ἀγχέμαχος is ‘close-fighting’ (ἄγχι ‘near’ + μάχη). The unit is cut at the comma.

sentences.t:
γνῷ δὲ καὶ Ἀτρεΐδης εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
ἣν ἄτην, ὅ τ’ ἄριστον Ἀχαιῶν οὐδὲν ἔτισεν.
sentences.l:
and may know also Atreus’-son, wide-ruling Agamemnon,
his own bewilderment, that the best of the Achaeans he honoured not at all.”
sentences.i: and so that Agamemnon, wide-ruling son of Atreus, may know his own bewilderment, that he paid no honour at all to the best of the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: γνῷ is the aorist subjunctive of γιγνώσκω, a second purpose joined by δέ to the one at line 271, and its subject is Ἀτρεΐδης … Ἀγαμέμνων with the stock εὐρὺ κρείων ‘wide-ruling’, printed as two words. ἣν is the possessive ‘his own’, and ἄτη is ‘bewilderment’, the clouding of the mind that brings ruin. ὅ τ’ (= ὅ τε) is ‘that’ and gives the content of the ἄτη, his failure to honour Achilles. ἔτισεν is the aorist of τίω ‘honour’. The lines stand also at 1.411–412. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ὄτρυνε μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἑκάστου,
ἐν δ’ ἔπεσον Τρώεσσιν ἀολλέες·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, he urged on the might and the heart of each man,
and they fell upon the Trojans, in a close mass;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and urged on the might and the heart of each man, and they fell upon the Trojans in a close mass;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes Patroclus’ speech, and line 275 has the words of line 210, but here it ends with a comma, so the sentence runs on. ἐν δ’ ἔπεσον is ‘and they fell upon’, ἐν set apart from ἔπεσον, the aorist of πίπτω; Τρώεσσιν is the epic dative plural, ‘upon the Trojans’. ἀολλέες ‘in a close mass’ is nominative plural and agrees with the Myrmidons. A new paragraph begins at 275. The ano teleia ends the unit mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δὲ νῆες
σμερδαλέον κονάβησαν ἀϋσάντων ὑπ’ Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
and around, the ships
frightfully rang under the Achaeans shouting.
sentences.i: and all around the ships rang frightfully at the shouting of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ δέ is ‘and around’, with ἀμφί an adverb. νῆες ‘ships’ is the subject of κονάβησαν, the aorist of κοναβέω ‘ring, resound’, and σμερδαλέον ‘frightfully’ is adverbial. ἀϋσάντων ὑπ’ Ἀχαιῶν is ‘at the shouting of the Achaeans’, ὑπό with the genitive of cause and ἀϋσάντων the aorist participle of ἀΰω ‘shout’. The two lines stand also at 2.333–334, where the Argives shout; the unit begins in the middle of line 276.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δ’ ὡς εἴδοντο Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμον υἱὸν
αὐτὸν καὶ θεράποντα σὺν ἔντεσι μαρμαίροντας,
sentences.l:
And the Trojans, when they saw Menoetius’ sturdy son,
himself and his attendant, in their gear gleaming,
sentences.i: And when the Trojans saw the sturdy son of Menoetius himself and his attendant gleaming in their gear,
sentences.n: ὡς εἴδοντο is ‘when they saw’, the middle form of the aorist of εἶδον, used with the active sense. Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμον υἱόν is ‘Menoetius’ sturdy son’, Patroclus, who is not named. αὐτὸν καὶ θεράποντα is ‘himself and his attendant’; the attendant is Automedon, who was named with him at line 219. σὺν ἔντεσι is ‘with their gear’ (ἔντεα, the fighting gear), and μαρμαίροντας ‘gleaming’ is accusative and agrees with both men.

sentences.t:
πᾶσιν ὀρίνθη θυμός, ἐκίνηθεν δὲ φάλαγγες
ἐλπόμενοι παρὰ ναῦφι ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα
μηνιθμὸν μὲν ἀπορρῖψαι, φιλότητα δ’ ἑλέσθαι·
sentences.i: the heart was stirred in all of them, and the battle-lines shook, in the hope that the fleet-footed son of Peleus had cast off his wrath beside the ships, and chosen friendship;
sentences.n: πᾶσιν ὀρίνθη θυμός is ‘in all of them the heart was stirred’: ὀρίνθη is the aorist passive of ὀρίνω ‘stir up’, and πᾶσιν the dative of those affected. ἐκίνηθεν (for ἐκινήθησαν) is ‘were moved’, with φάλαγγες ‘battle-lines’ as subject. ἐλπόμενοι ‘hoping’ is masculine though φάλαγγες is feminine, because it means the men in them. Its infinitives ἀπορρῖψαι ‘to have cast off’ and ἑλέσθαι ‘to have chosen’ are aorists, referring to what they hope Achilles has already done. ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα ‘the fleet-footed son of Peleus’ is Achilles, and μηνιθμὸν μὲν … φιλότητα δ’ sets wrath against friendship.

sentences.t: πάπτηνεν δὲ ἕκαστος ὅπῃ φύγοι αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον.
sentences.l: and each looked about where he might flee steep destruction.
sentences.i: and each of them looked about for some way to escape steep destruction.
sentences.n: πάπτηνεν is the aorist of παπταίνω ‘look about’, without the augment, and ἕκαστος ‘each one’ is its subject. ὅπῃ φύγοι is an indirect question with the optative, ‘where he might flee’, and αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον ‘steep destruction’ is the object of φύγοι. The line stands also at 14.507 and at Odyssey 22.43.

sentences.t:
Πάτροκλος δὲ πρῶτος ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ
ἀντικρὺ κατὰ μέσσον, ὅθι πλεῖστοι κλονέοντο,
νηῒ πάρα πρυμνῇ μεγαθύμου Πρωτεσιλάου,
sentences.l:
And Patroclus first cast with his shining spear
straight into the middle, where most were being thrown into confusion,
beside the stern of the ship of great-hearted Protesilaus,
sentences.i: And Patroclus was the first to cast his shining spear, straight into the middle where the most of them were being thrown into confusion, beside the stern of the ship of great-hearted Protesilaus,
sentences.n: πρῶτος ‘first’ is a predicate, ‘was first to cast’. ἀκόντισε is the aorist of ἀκοντίζω ‘cast a spear’, with the dative δουρὶ φαεινῷ ‘with his shining spear’. ἀντικρύ is ‘straight’, and κατὰ μέσσον ‘into the middle’ has the epic spelling μέσσον. ὅθι ‘where’ gives the place, the thick of the Trojans, where πλεῖστοι κλονέοντο ‘most were being thrown into confusion’. νηῒ πάρα πρυμνῇ is ‘beside the stern of the ship’, with πάρα placed after its noun; μεγαθύμου Πρωτεσιλάου ‘of great-hearted Protesilaus’ names whose ship it is. The unit is cut at the comma.

sentences.t:
καὶ βάλε Πυραίχμην, ὃς Παίονας ἱπποκορυστὰς
ἤγαγεν ἐξ Ἀμυδῶνος ἀπ’ Ἀξιοῦ εὐρὺ ῥέοντος·
sentences.l:
and struck Pyraechmes, who the Paeonians, horse-arming,
led from Amydon, from the Axius flowing wide;
sentences.i: and struck Pyraechmes, who led the Paeonians, armed with horses, from Amydon, from the wide-flowing Axius;
sentences.n: καὶ βάλε Πυραίχμην is ‘and struck Pyraechmes’, and the relative clause ὃς … ἤγαγεν (the aorist of ἄγω) says who he was. Παίονας ἱπποκορυστάς is ‘the Paeonians armed with horses’: ἱπποκορυστής is built on ἵππος ‘horse’ and κορύσσω ‘arm’, and whether it means chariot-fighters or men with horsehair-crested helmets is not known. ἐξ Ἀμυδῶνος ἀπ’ Ἀξιοῦ is ‘from Amydon, from the Axius’, a river; εὐρὺ ῥέοντος ‘wide-flowing’ is its genitive participle. The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t: τὸν βάλε δεξιὸν ὦμον·
sentences.l: him he struck on the right shoulder;
sentences.i: he struck him in the right shoulder;
sentences.n: τὸν βάλε repeats the verb of the line before to say where the blow fell: τόν ‘him’ is Pyraechmes, and δεξιὸν ὦμον ‘right shoulder’ is an accusative of respect, ‘in the right shoulder’. The unit is short because an ano teleia follows ὦμον in the middle of line 289.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὕπτιος ἐν κονίῃσι
κάππεσεν οἰμώξας, ἕταροι δέ μιν ἀμφεφόβηθεν
Παίονες·
sentences.i: and he fell on his back in the dust, wailing, and his companions, the Paeonians, were thrown into panic about him;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ (ὁ as a pronoun) is Pyraechmes. ὕπτιος ‘on his back’ and ἐν κονίῃσι ‘in the dust’ (plural, epic dative) describe his fall, and κάππεσεν is κατέπεσεν, the aorist of καταπίπτω, with κατά assimilated to the π. οἰμώξας is the aorist participle of οἰμώζω ‘wail’. ἀμφεφόβηθεν is a rare aorist passive (-θεν for -θησαν), built on ἀμφί ‘around’ and φοβέω ‘frighten’, and the sense ‘were thrown into panic around him’ is taken from its parts. Παίονες, after the verb, names the companions.

sentences.t:
ἐν γὰρ Πάτροκλος φόβον ἧκεν ἅπασιν
ἡγεμόνα κτείνας, ὃς ἀριστεύεσκε μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
for among them all Patroclus cast terror,
having killed the leader, who used to be the best at fighting.
sentences.i: for Patroclus cast terror among them all by killing their leader, who used to be the best at fighting.
sentences.n: ἐν … ἧκεν is ‘cast among’, ἐν set apart from ἧκεν, the aorist of ἵημι ‘send, throw’; φόβον ‘terror’ is its object and ἅπασιν ‘among them all’ the dative. γάρ gives the reason for the panic. ἡγεμόνα κτείνας is ‘having killed the leader’, and the aorist participle says how the terror was cast. ὃς ἀριστεύεσκε μάχεσθαι is ‘who used to be the best at fighting’: ἀριστεύεσκε is the iterative imperfect of ἀριστεύω ‘be the best’, with the infinitive μάχεσθαι.

sentences.t: ἐκ νηῶν δ’ ἔλασεν, κατὰ δ’ ἔσβεσεν αἰθόμενον πῦρ.
sentences.l: And from the ships he drove, and quenched the burning fire.
sentences.i: And he drove them away from the ships and put out the burning fire.
sentences.n: Patroclus is still the subject. ἐκ νηῶν δ’ ἔλασεν is ‘and drove from the ships’: ἔλασεν is the aorist of ἐλαύνω, and the Greek does not state its object, which is the enemy. κατὰ δ’ ἔσβεσεν is ‘and quenched’, with κατά set apart from the verb, and αἰθόμενον πῦρ ‘the burning fire’ is its object, αἰθόμενον the participle of αἴθω ‘burn’.

sentences.t: ἡμιδαὴς δ’ ἄρα νηῦς λίπετ’ αὐτόθι·
sentences.l: And half-burnt, then, the ship was left there;
sentences.i: And the ship was left there half-burnt;
sentences.n: ἡμιδαής ‘half-burnt’ is built on ἡμι- ‘half’ and the root of δαίω ‘burn’, and νηῦς is the epic nominative of ναῦς ‘ship’. λίπετ’ is λίπετο, the aorist middle of λείπω without the augment, ‘was left’, and αὐτόθι is ‘there’, on the spot. ἄρα ‘then’ marks it as the result of what Patroclus did. The unit is short because the ano teleia falls after αὐτόθι, in the middle of line 294.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δὲ φόβηθεν
Τρῶες θεσπεσίῳ ὁμάδῳ·
sentences.l:
and they were put to flight,
the Trojans, with wondrous uproar;
sentences.i: and the Trojans fled with a wondrous uproar;
sentences.n: τοὶ δέ ‘and they’ (τοί is the article used as a pronoun) is made definite by Τρῶες in the next line. φόβηθεν is the aorist passive of φοβέω, ‘were put to flight’ (-θεν for -θησαν), as at 12.470. θεσπεσίῳ ὁμάδῳ is ‘with a wondrous uproar’, a dative of manner; ὅμαδος is the din a crowd makes. The ano teleia ends the unit mid-line.

sentences.t:
Δαναοὶ δ’ ἐπέχυντο
νῆας ἀνὰ γλαφυράς·
sentences.l:
and the Danaans poured themselves
up among the hollow ships;
sentences.i: and the Danaans poured out among the hollow ships;
sentences.n: Δαναοί ‘Danaans’ is the poet’s name here for the army that holds the ships. ἐπέχυντο is an aorist of ἐπιχέω ‘pour upon’, in the middle form with a passive sense, of men who spread out like a flood; it is the same verb as ἐξεχέοντο at 259 with a different preverb. νῆας ἀνὰ γλαφυράς is ‘up among the hollow ships’, ἀνά with the accusative, and the words stand also at 12.470–471. The ano teleia ends the unit mid-line.

sentences.t: ὅμαδος δ’ ἀλίαστος ἐτύχθη.
sentences.l: and an uproar, relentless, was made.
sentences.i: and a relentless uproar arose.
sentences.n: ὅμαδος is a din or uproar, and ἀλίαστος ‘relentless’ (its origin is uncertain). ἐτύχθη is the aorist passive of τεύχω, ‘was made, came about’. The half-line stands also at 12.471.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἀφ’ ὑψηλῆς κορυφῆς ὄρεος μεγάλοιο
κινήσῃ πυκινὴν νεφέλην στεροπηγερέτα Ζεύς,
sentences.l:
And as when from the high peak of a great mountain
moves a solid cloud the lightning-gatherer Zeus,
sentences.i: And as when, from the high peak of a great mountain, Zeus who gathers the lightning stirs a dense cloud,
sentences.n: A new simile begins. ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ‘and as when’ takes the subjunctive κινήσῃ, from κινέω ‘move’, with πυκινὴν νεφέλην ‘a dense cloud’ as its object; ἀφ’ ὑψηλῆς κορυφῆς ὄρεος μεγάλοιο is ‘from the high peak of a great mountain’, ὄρεος the epic genitive of ὄρος. στεροπηγερέτα is a stock epithet of Zeus, built on στεροπή ‘lightning’ and the root of ἀγείρω ‘gather’, like νεφεληγερέτα ‘who gathers the clouds’, with the same epic nominative in -α. It is translated every time. The unit is cut at the comma.

sentences.t:
ἔκ τ’ ἔφανεν πᾶσαι σκοπιαὶ καὶ πρώονες ἄκροι
καὶ νάπαι, οὐρανόθεν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπερράγη ἄσπετος αἰθήρ,
sentences.l:
and show forth all the lookout-peaks and the headlands, the high ones,
and the dells, and from heaven bursts open the boundless aether,
sentences.i: and all the lookout peaks and high headlands and dells come into view, and from heaven the boundless upper air bursts open,
sentences.n: Lines 299–300 repeat 8.557–558, where the picture is of stars. ἔκ τ’ … ἔφανεν is the epic third-person plural (for ἐφάνησαν) with its preverb apart, ‘shone forth’; the aorist states what always happens, so the English puts it in the present. σκοπιαί are peaks from which one looks out, πρώονες jutting headlands (ἄκροι ‘high’), and νάπαι wooded dells. ὑπερράγη is the aorist passive of a compound of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’, ‘burst open’, again put in the present; ἄσπετος is ‘boundless’, and αἰθήρ the bright upper air.

sentences.t:
ὣς Δαναοὶ νηῶν μὲν ἀπωσάμενοι δήϊον πῦρ
τυτθὸν ἀνέπνευσαν, πολέμου δ’ οὐ γίγνετ’ ἐρωή·
sentences.l:
so the Danaans, having thrust from the ships the hostile fire,
breathed again a little, but of the war there was no respite;
sentences.i: so the Danaans, having thrust the hostile fire from the ships, drew breath again for a little while, but there was no respite from the war;
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ answers the simile. νηῶν μὲν ἀπωσάμενοι δήϊον πῦρ is ‘having thrust the hostile fire from the ships’, ἀπωσάμενοι the aorist middle participle of ἀπωθέω and δήϊον ‘hostile’; the μέν looks to the δέ clause, setting what is gained against what is not. τυτθόν ‘a little’ goes with ἀνέπνευσαν, the aorist of ἀναπνέω ‘draw breath again’. πολέμου δ’ οὐ γίγνετ’ ἐρωή is ‘of the war there came no respite’: γίγνετ’ is γίγνετο, the imperfect without the augment, and ἐρωή here is a letting-up, a sense taken from the context.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πώ τι Τρῶες ἀρηϊφίλων ὑπ’ Ἀχαιῶν
προτροπάδην φοβέοντο μελαινάων ἀπὸ νηῶν,
ἀλλ’ ἔτ’ ἄρ’ ἀνθίσταντο, νεῶν δ’ ὑπόεικον ἀνάγκῃ.
sentences.l:
for not yet in any way were the Trojans by the Ares-loved Achaeans
headlong being put to flight from the black ships,
but still they stood against them, and gave way from the ships under compulsion.
sentences.i: for the Trojans were not yet being put to flight headlong from the black ships by the Achaeans, dear to Ares, but still they stood their ground against them, and gave way from the ships under compulsion.
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ πώ τι is ‘for not yet at all’, and gives the reason there was no respite. Τρῶες … ὑπ’ Ἀχαιῶν is ‘the Trojans … by the Achaeans’, with ἀρηϊφίλων ‘dear to Ares’ as a stock epithet of the Achaeans. προτροπάδην ‘headlong’ is an adverb, and φοβέοντο the imperfect passive of φοβέω ‘put to flight’; μελαινάων is the epic genitive plural of μέλας, ‘from the black ships’. ἀνθίσταντο is ‘stood against’, and ὑπόεικον the imperfect of ὑπείκω ‘give way’, taking the genitive νεῶν (a second epic form of the genitive plural of ναῦς, beside νηῶν) with the dative ἀνάγκῃ ‘by necessity’.
